Experiments cover increasing object counts, composition of previously demonstrated skills, different planning budgets, and stronger reasoning models. These provide evidence of useful generalization within the evaluated environments.
Deployments on three robot platforms provide qualitative evidence of practical feasibility. The appendix supplies useful prompt templates and additional experimental results.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not adequately establish the contribution over prior domain-learning methods. Most baselines generate plans directly with LLMs, whereas PDDLLM uses a symbolic solver. RuleAsMem primarily demonstrates the benefit of that solver. Comparisons with relevant domain-induction approaches, using matched planning backends and explicit input assumptions, are missing. Ablations also do not isolate simulation filtering, predicate invention, action induction, or LoCA.

The automatic grounding claim is technically underspecified. Section 5.2 retrieves first-order effect constraints, but does not explain sufficiently how negative and quantified effects, grasp/release transitions, or preservation of other required relations are handled. Satisfying endpoint inequalities alone does not establish the claimed guarantee of semantically correct manipulation. A complete constraint-compilation and execution formulation is needed to assess this central contribution.

The single-demonstration and minimal-engineering claims require qualification. Rearrangement combines stacking and unstacking demonstrations, while bridge building combines stacking and alignment demonstrations (Section A.10.1). The system also assumes structured object states, selected feature ranges and partitions, a physical simulator, and thousands of simulated samples; real demonstrations use CAD information and markers. These are legitimate assumptions, but the reduction in total human engineering effort is not measured.

Important details remain missing for reproducibility and evaluation validity: feature partition settings, simulation sampling budgets and feasibility criteria, action extraction and consolidation procedures, and candidate-domain acceptance rules. Section 5.1.3 does not identify which problems guide candidate replacement or establish their separation from evaluation tasks. It is also unclear whether the three runs independently regenerate domains. The expert reference is constructed by editing generated domains, limiting the independence of the domain-quality assessment.

The efficiency evidence needs clearer accounting. Appendix A.6 attributes fast online planning to offline domain inference, but does not report total offline simulation and generation time or the workload needed to amortize it. Table 2 does not establish uniformly lower token consumption: PDDLLM uses more tokens than LLMTAMP in all three domains, and its Hanoi token count exceeds both reasoning baselines. The claims should distinguish online latency, preparation cost, and success-versus-cost tradeoffs.

Real-robot validation lacks trial counts, aggregate success rates, comparative results, and failure analysis. The VLA experiment additionally uses 200 fine-tuning trajectories and bypasses explicit motion constraints, offering limited evidence for LoCA itself. Likewise, the 'noisy' demonstration experiment adds a valid but irrelevant unstack action; it does not establish robustness to measurement noise, unsuccessful actions, or corrupted trajectories.

Table 15 reports an 8.3% domain-generation failure rate at the default ten prompts, without explaining how these failures enter the headline success rates. Important reproduction details remain missing despite the extensive appendix: simulation sampling budgets and feasibility criteria, the finite grammar or depth limit for higher-order predicate enumeration, and executable domain/interface artifacts. The system assumes structured object features, CAD/URDF models, reliable state estimates, and a simulator; the rearrangement and bridge-building experiments use two demonstrations. These assumptions are reasonable, but the evidence supports a narrower claim than general, fully automated domain construction from one demonstration.

strengths: Addresses an important robotics problem: reducing manual construction of symbolic planning domains. Combining simulation-grounded predicates, demonstration-based action induction, and reusable symbolic planning is a promising system design.

Reports substantial gains across over 1,200 problems in nine task categories: 93.3% overall success versus 52.5% for the strongest GPT-4o direct-planning baseline, approaching the expert reference at 95.7%.

The appendices provide useful experiments on prompt variation, discretization, planning budgets, alternative LLM backbones, and perception noise. Composing domains from simpler demonstrations is also a useful capability.
Physical deployment provides evidence beyond simulation: four task/platform combinations achieve 7–9 successes in ten trials, spanning three robot platforms.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish the central domain-learning contribution. Baselines predominantly generate plans directly with LLMs; outperforming them mainly demonstrates the benefit of symbolic search. There are no empirical comparisons against closely related domain-learning approaches such as Guan et al. (2023) or Huang et al. (2025), nor a control that generates domains from the same inputs without simulation. RuleAsMem does not isolate these contributions.

The claimed correctness guarantee for LoCA in Section 5.2 is unsupported. Converting action effects into geometric inequalities does not by itself establish correct grasp/release transitions, preservation of unaffected predicates, or consistency of negative and quantified predicates. Likewise, finding a feasible sample within a discretized region does not establish feasibility throughout that region. The manuscript needs a precise interface specification and validation of these cases to substantiate its central automation claim.

The evaluation protocol leaves important uncertainty about domain construction and selection. Sections 5.1.3 and B.7 filter candidate domains using execution outcomes without clearly specifying separate validation problems. Table 15 reports an 8.3% domain-generation failure rate at the default ten prompts, contradicting the nearby claim of consistent success; whether these failures enter the headline planning results is unclear. Additionally, expert domains are refinements of generated domains, making the missing/redundant-predicate comparison dependent on the method being evaluated.

The single-demonstration and automation claims need narrower scope. Rearrangement and bridge building use multiple subtask demonstrations, while the system assumes structured state features, CAD/URDF information, tracked object poses, and an available simulator. These are legitimate assumptions, but the paper does not quantify the remaining engineering effort. The VLA deployment additionally uses 200 fine-tuning trajectories and therefore provides compatibility evidence rather than evidence for learning the complete system from one demonstration.

Efficiency claims require clearer accounting. Online planning times exclude domain derivation, which consumes approximately 334,000–535,000 tokens for the three reported domains, alongside simulation work. Complete preprocessing runtimes and explicit amortization over repeated problems are missing. Token savings are also not uniform: Table 2 shows higher PDDLLM token costs than both reasoning baselines on Hanoi and bridge building.

Reproducibility remains insufficient despite the extensive appendix. The manuscript does not identify a code/data release or provide complete executable domains and the LoCA implementation. Simulation sampling and feasibility criteria, bounds on higher-order predicate enumeration, and compilation of the informal quantified expressions remain underspecified. These omissions prevent independent verification of the most technically consequential components.
